title: OAuth flows, connected apps, external credentials, named credentials, and token safety

objectives: Describe OAuth 2.0 as token-based authorization via a connected app or external client app, using the official three-step model—without inventing grant parameter lists.
Choose connected-app inbound access versus named credentials plus external credentials for outbound callouts.
State that user external credentials store encrypted tokens and that Apex should use callout named credentials instead of hardcoded secrets.
Name only OAuth flows that Salesforce Help documents, and send grant details to that page.
diagnostic_question: A middleware app must call Salesforce REST, and Apex must call GitHub. Where do connected apps vs named/external credentials belong, and where must tokens never live?
definition: OAuth 2.0 is an open protocol that authorizes sharing Salesforce (or remote) data through tokens rather than handing over a password to every client. A connected app (or external client app) requests access; an authorizing server issues tokens; a resource server validates them. For Salesforce callouts, a named credential holds the endpoint URL and HTTP transport; an external credential holds the authentication protocol and principals; user external credentials store encrypted tokens. ([Authorize Apps with OAuth](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=remoteaccess_authenticate.htm); [Named Credentials](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/named-credentials/guide/get-started.html); [OAuth and connected apps](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api.meta/api/sforce_api_oauth_and_connected_apps.htm))
why_it_matters: Hard-coded tokens in Apex, username-password 'because it is faster,' and over-scoped connected apps are interview and incident failures. Token safety is the difference between a managed secret and a leaked session.
sixty_second_explanation: Think of a bonded warehouse. A connected app is a registered visitor company. An OAuth flow is how the gate issues a time-limited badge (token) after the right dance—look up the dance in Salesforce Help, do not invent it. Named credentials are the labeled truck route to someone else's warehouse. External credentials are how that truck proves itself. Encrypted user external credentials are the badge locker. Apex should ask the locker, not tape badges to the windshield.
deeper_explanation: Official three steps for an OAuth authorization flow: the client (via connected app or external client app) requests access; the authorizing server grants access tokens; the resource server validates tokens and allows the protected resource. Details of each supported flow are in Salesforce Help: OAuth Authorization Flows. This lesson will not invent grant_type values, endpoint query strings, or token lifetimes. ([SOAP/REST OAuth topics](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api.meta/api/sforce_api_oauth_and_connected_apps.htm))

Help articles that configure connected apps mention enabling OAuth settings, selecting OAuth scopes (see OAuth Tokens and Scopes), optional PKCE for supported authorization-code style flows, and separate configuration topics for the OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials Flow and the Authorization Code and Credentials Flow. If an interviewer asks for a full grant catalog, open Help—do not recitation-invent. ([Enable OAuth Settings](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=connected_app_create_api_integration.htm))

Named credentials (preferred, post-Winter '23 model): named credential = callout endpoint + HTTP transport; external credential = authentication protocol and principals; the same external credential can serve multiple named credentials; principals map to permission sets/profiles; user external credentials store encrypted tokens. Legacy named credentials are deprecated and slated for discontinuation. ([Get Started with Named Credentials](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/named-credentials/guide/get-started.html))

Token safety: do not put access tokens, refresh tokens, or client secrets in Apex source, debug logs, or LAB_ fields. Prefer named credentials so Salesforce generates the authorization header. Rotate and revoke via Setup/connected-app policies. Exact refresh behavior is flow-specific—Needs verification on the Help page for that flow.

claims.claim: OAuth 2.0 authorizes secure data sharing through tokens. Connected apps or external client apps request access using an OAuth 2.0 flow. Official general steps: request access, authorizing server grants tokens, resource server validates tokens.
claims.validation: Authorize Apps with OAuth and SOAP API OAuth topic.

claims.claim: Per-flow procedures and parameters are documented in Salesforce Help OAuth Authorization Flows. This handbook does not invent grant details. Help for connected apps also documents OAuth scopes, an optional PKCE requirement for supported authorization-code style flows, and separate setup for Client Credentials and Authorization Code and Credentials flows.
claims.validation: Developer guide defers to Help; Enable OAuth Settings names those flows without this lesson copying parameter tables.

claims.claim: A named credential specifies a callout endpoint and HTTP transport. An external credential supplies authentication protocol and principals. User external credentials store encrypted tokens. The same external credential can be reused by more than one named credential. Legacy named credentials are deprecated in favor of this model introduced Winter '23.
OAuth scopes on a connected app define the protected resources tokens may access. Identity URL is available when the id scope is authorized in user-agent or web server flows as documented in Help.
claims.validation: Authorize Apps with OAuth; Enable OAuth Settings.

changed_in_release: Prefer new named/external credentials over legacy named credentials. Reverify External Client Apps vs connected-app creation policy in the target org for Summer '26—Needs verification, do not invent a cutoff date here.
unresolved_uncertainty: Exact token lifetimes, endpoint paths, and grant_type strings are flow-specific—use OAuth Authorization Flows Help.

interview_explanation.thirty_seconds: Inbound: connected app or external client app plus an OAuth flow from Help. Outbound: named credential for the URL, external credential for auth, encrypted user external credentials for tokens. I never paste tokens into Apex, and I do not invent grant parameter lists.
interview_explanation.two_minutes: OAuth 2.0 exchanges tokens, not a shared password taped in code. I can recite the three official steps. For which dance to use, I name only flows Help names—web server, PKCE for supported authorization-code style flows, client credentials, Authorization Code and Credentials—and I send details to OAuth Authorization Flows. Scopes bound the badge. Named credentials skip embedding secrets and can skip remote site settings for that host. Legacy named credentials should not be the default after Winter '23.

interview_questions.question: How do OAuth, connected apps, named credentials, and token safety fit together?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: OAuth issues tokens for apps. Connected apps (or external client apps) are inbound registration. Named plus external credentials are outbound. Tokens stay encrypted, never in Apex.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I draw two arrows. They call Salesforce: OAuth 2.0 three steps, scopes, Help for the flow. We call them: named credential URL, external credential protocol, user external credentials encrypted. Token safety is least scope, no logs, no git. I will not recite invented grant_type tables.
interview_questions.example: Middleware inbound REST plus Apex outbound to a test HTTP API in sandbox.

interview_questions.question: An interviewer asks you to list every OAuth grant Salesforce supports with POST bodies. What do you do?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I refuse to invent. I name Help: OAuth Authorization Flows, plus Help-mentioned families like web server, client credentials, Authorization Code and Credentials, PKCE. Details stay on those pages.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: The SOAP/REST developer topics explicitly say to apply a flow after reviewing Help. Invented password grants are a red flag. I can still explain the three steps and inbound vs outbound.
interview_questions.example: Whiteboard with a link-out box labeled Help instead of fake JSON.
follow_ups: What if they insist on grant_type?

interview_questions.question: Apex currently sets a Bearer header from a Custom Label. Redesign.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Create named credential and external credential; switch endpoint to callout:; delete the label; never log the old token; revoke it.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Official named credentials exist so code does not manage authentication. User external credentials hold encrypted tokens. I add principal permissions so only the integration profile can call out. INT-006 is the send() lab.
interview_questions.example: LAB_HttpBin named credential replacing a leaked label.

interview_questions.question: Product wants a connected app with every OAuth scope 'to save time.'
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I refuse. Scopes define token reach. Least privilege, documented in OAuth Tokens and Scopes Help.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Enable OAuth Settings is where scopes are chosen. Over-scoping turns a stolen token into a wider incident. I still will not invent scope string tables; I will open Help in the review.
interview_questions.example: Sandbox app that only needs api to LAB_ objects.

interview_questions.question: Outbound callout 401 after rotating a remote client secret.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Update the external credential/principal secret via documented Setup or Connect API; do not paste the secret into Apex to test.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Named credential still points at the URL; auth material lives on the external credential. Packaging guides note secrets are not packaged. I check generate authorization header and principal access. I re-auth named or per-user principal as the identity type requires.
interview_questions.example: GitHub app secret rotated; Apex unchanged and still using callout:.

interview_questions.question: Inbound integration 401 in production, 200 in sandbox.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Different connected app, callback, secret, username, or my-domain. Tokens are environment-specific. I do not copy production tokens into sandbox logs.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I compare OAuth usage, login history, and scopes. I look up the flow's refresh rules in Help rather than guessing expiry seconds. I check IP relaxation and policies on the connected app.
interview_questions.example: CI still using sandbox client id against prod host.

interview_questions.question: When named principal versus per-user principal on an external credential?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Named principal: one identity for all users of that callout. Per-user: each user authorizes; callouts use that user's token. I will not invent protocol-specific claim tables.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Get Started and the OAuth named-credential guide distinguish identity types. Packaging examples mention named vs per-user for basic auth and OAuth variants. I pick named for a shared org-level ERP and per-user when the remote system must see the human.
interview_questions.example: Org-wide markdown converter vs per-user GitHub gists (from named-credential examples).

interview_questions.question: Teach the bonded-warehouse analogy and where it breaks.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Connected app is a registered company, OAuth flow is the badge dance from Help, named credential is the truck route, external credential is the proof, encrypted cabinet holds badges. It breaks if I pretend the dance steps are in the analogy.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I emphasize inbound vs outbound docks. I say PKCE and client-secret rules are Help, not warehouse folklore. Legacy named credentials are old paper forms being retired, and I will not invent grant_type bodies or token TTLs.
interview_questions.example: Two-arrow whiteboard: they call us vs we call them.
